title: Eyes Above the Honesty Box
text:
In a psychology department at Newcastle University in England, staff paid for their tea, coffee and milk by putting money into an honesty box in the shared kitchen. A notice above the box listed the prices. No one checked who paid.

Melissa Bateson, Daniel Nettle and Gilbert Roberts quietly ran an experiment. For ten weeks, they changed a small image at the top of the price notice each week. In some weeks, the image showed a pair of human eyes, looking at the viewer. In alternating weeks, it showed flowers. Nothing else changed. Each week, they recorded how much money was in the box and how much milk had been used, as a measure of how much drink had been consumed.

In the weeks with eyes, people paid nearly three times as much per liter of milk as in the weeks with flowers. The amount paid rose and fell with the image, week by week.

The authors suggested that even a picture of eyes may trigger an automatic sense of being watched, and that people behave more cooperatively when they feel their reputation might be at stake.
lesson: People contribute more to shared goods when they feel seen. Make cooperation in a team visible, so that contributing is noticed.
people: Melissa Bateson, Daniel Nettle, Gilbert Roberts
location: Newcastle University, Newcastle upon Tyne, UK
source: Bateson, M., Nettle, D., and Roberts, G. (2006). Cues of being watched enhance cooperation in a real-world setting. Biology Letters, 2(3), 412-414.
caveat: Later studies and meta-analyses have found that watching eyes images have small or unreliable effects on generosity, though some effects on other behaviors remain.
